speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the house will recall that on February 9 I tabled the text of the Soviet note of January 10 to the Canadian government proposing 

a conference of 28 countries, including Canada, to consider a peace treaty with Germany. At the same time I tabled a copy of the draft peace treaty which accompanied the Soviet note.
I now inform the house that the Canadian reply to the Soviet government's note was today handed to the Soviet embassy in Ottawa, and our ambassador to the U.S.S.R. was instructed to deliver a copy to the appropriate authorities in Moscow.
I take this opportunity of tabling copies of the Canadian reply. As members will note, it reflects the government's view that the many questions raised in the Soviet note could most profitably be examined at a conference on all aspects of the German question, in which the four powers who have special responsibilities for Germany, the U.S.S.R., France, the United Kingdom and the United States, would participate. Until the results of this four power meeting have been assessed it would not be useful to take a decision about the holding of a large peace treaty conference attended by Canada and other participants in the war against Germany.
As reported in the press, Mr. Speaker, the governments of France, the United Kingdom, the United States and West Germany yesterday sent their replies to the Soviet goverment's notes of January 10 proposing a German peace treaty. These replies were considered last week in the NATO council, where the attitudes of other NATO members to the Soviet proposals were also discussed. Although differing somewhat in detail, the replies of the four powers are essentially at one in proposing a meeting in the spring of the foreign ministers of the U.S.S.R., France, the United Kingdom and the United States to discuss all aspects of the German problem.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Might I ask the minister whether the four power reply to which he has just referred was considered by the members of the NATO council before it was agreed upon?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The answer is yes, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government has been kept informed of the negotiations between the United Kingdom and the Greek and Turkish governments for an agreed

and peaceful settlement of the Cyprus question, which I am sure everyone in this house earnestly hopes will be achieved; and would the Prime Minister be in a position to make a statement in regard to the negotiations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROGRESS OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition gave me notice of this question, which enables me to give an immediate reply. I cannot, of course, report on the negotiations for an agreed and peaceful solution to the Cyprus question at this time, in view of the fact that the formal tripartite conference seeking to achieve such a solution began its deliberations in London only this morning.
Reports have been received of the discussions which the prime ministers of Greece and Turkey concluded at Zurich last week. They indicate that progress appears to have been made toward a solution of the problem, that there has been a favourable reaction to the Zurich talks in the United Kingdom and Cyprus, and that the results of these talks have at least been accepted as a basis for negotiation at the conference in London. The Canadian government and its partners in the NATO council are hopeful that the negotiations being conducted in London will lead to a just and lasting solution to this complex problem which involves three of our NATO allies.
Today, according to a dispatch, the British foreign secretary, Right Hon. Selwyn Lloyd, announced that there were four factors which are considered by the British government to be basic to any solution of this problem namely: The strategic interests of the United Kingdom in Cyprus must be safeguarded in such a way that they cannot be compromised in the future; the two Cypriot communities must be reconciled; Greco-Turkish friendship must be re-established; the Cypriots themselves must be given the opportunity to establish their own institutions.
Further than that I do not think it is possible to go at this moment.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RENEWAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 6 I informed the house that the service that had been prevailing between Australia and Canada in respect to air flights had been extended from February 10 to March 11, and I assured the house at that time that Canada was pressing for a continuation of that service. The air agreement between Canada and Australia was signed at Ottawa on June 11, 1946 and it provides for direct air services oetween the two countries. From time to time discussions have taken place as to the frequency and capacity of flights for this direct air service. The frequencies are controlled by licences issued under the agreement by the aeronautical authorities of both countries, and the air agreement has been interpreted somewhat differently in this regard by Canada and Australia.
As I informed the house on February 6, discussions are now taking place with Australia to resolve these licensing difficulties, and every effort will be made by the government to maintain reasonable conditions for the Canadian air carrier operating over this route.

speechtext: 709. Payments to a province during 1958-59 and 1959-60 fiscal years in accordance with an agreement entered into by the government of Canada and the province, with the approval of the governor in council, that provides for contributions by the government of Canada of amounts not exceeding one half of the cost of labour incurred in the period from the 1st day of December, 1958, to the 30th day of April, 1959, on winter work projects in municipalities as contemplated by the agreement, $15,000,000.
Mr. Chairman, when last we had this item before us I was indicating-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I wonder if those members who are leaving the house would please do so quietly so we may hear the hon. member who has the floor.

I was indicating on Friday of last week, when our consideration of this item was interrupted, that in my opinion

Supply-Labour
there are two serious national economic issues lacing us at this time. One is the matter of inflation, and the other is the matter of unemployment. I believe that is fairly well recognized in all parts of the house. We have not yet heard the government's program to deal with the matter of inflation. However, we hope to hear of that at the time the budget is presented.
We have here an indication that the program for dealing with unemployment is very limited indeed. The very name by which this matter is commonly known is an indication of the limited nature of the program that is being offered, because it is commonly referred to as the winter works program. Unemployment in Canada at the present time is much more serious than something that would be taken care of by merely a winter works program. We need a more basic solution than that.
However, even though this is the only specific solution being offered at this time, we in this group will not hesitate to support the vote of $15 million here requested. We feel that this program, limited though it is, would have been much more effective had it been offered to the provinces and to the municipalities much earlier. We regret also that the terms limit participation by the federal government in this relief project to a period of only five months of the year. We know from all indications, and especially in the light of the figures that were revealed only yesterday, that we will have a serious unemployment problem in the month of May, at which time this program will have ended.
We regret that the program is not extensive enough, and is very limited in the number and type of projects that can be included. We realize that the number of unemployed who are going to receive help, who are going to be supplied with employment under this measure, is a very small portion of the hundreds of thousands who are actually unemployed. We realize that this measure meets only to a small degree the larger needs of municipalities which they are hoping to meet by participation in this program.
Looking at the amount of money asked for, Mr. Chairman, and doing a little arithmetic of our own, we find that we are being asked for $15 million to supply assistance for five months. This means $3 million per month. The expectation of the minister is that normal wages are going to be paid, at least normal wages, and I am very pleased to note that he made mention of that. If we assume that $300 per month will be paid for the five months period, according to my arithmetic that only gives employment to about 10,000 men in Canada. If you have $15 million

divided by five and divided by $300 per month, you arrive at 10,000 men employed.
I fail to reconcile that with the very hopeful prediction of the minister last week when he indicated that with only half the money used thus far he was already assured of 22,712 men being employed. I hope the minister will at some later point be able to reconcile the great variation that exists between dividing $15 million by five, divided by $300 per month, resulting in 10,000 men being given assistance, and his statement. The minister told us that with apparently only half the expected projects in yet, and with only half the money being used, he already arrives at a figure twice as large as the one at which I arrived.
If we provide employment to 10,000 men of the 500,000 who are unemployed, we are only assisting 2 per cent of the unemployed of Canada. Even if the minister's prediction is borne out, and for every man given employment on-site there will be three men given employment off-site, we would only be giving assistance to about 8 per cent of the unemployed of Canada.
One of our major complaints about this program is that it involves a heavy and costly burden on our municipalities. There have been so many estimates made the portion of these projects which consists of labour costs that one finds it difficult to arrive at a decision. The minister gave us an estimate of some 38 per cent. I do not know what kind of a hat that particular forecast was grabbed from, but from the information I have been able to obtain from municipal officers in many parts of Canada, labour costs on these winter works projects will run from a low of 2J per cent to a high of 12 per cent.
When we consider that this offer means that Ottawa will pay only one-half the cost of labour, it means that the labour cost involved that Ottawa will pay in relation to the cost of the undertaking as a whole is somewhere from 1.25 per cent of the cost to a high of 6.25 per cent. To take the smaller figure, with $15 million on the part of the federal government this means that our municipalities, if they wish to take full advantage of this offer, will be obliged to expend the sum of $1,170 million; or even if we take the more optimistic forecast, namely that one eighth of the cost of these projects is labour content, then for the $15 million that Ottawa is willing to spend or is prepared to spend, our municipalities will be obliged to spend $210 million.
If these figures are anywhere nearly accurate, Mr. Chairman, then I must say at

this time that even the old municipal improvements assistance act which was instituted in the hungry thirties by a former government was of far greater value to the municipalities, both as a relief of unemployment measure and also as a local improvement measure, than this present winter works program.
I must say this. What is $15 million of an investment by this federal government when we consider the fantastic loss to the national wealth in having half a million people unemployed even for one day? In one day we lose $6 million of wealth as the result of half a million people being unemployed. If we keep half a million Canadians unemployed for the five months to which this item refers, then the national economy will have lost $600 million of wealth. Yet we have in office a government which in its efforts to avoid this huge loss as a result of unemployment can offer only $15 million.
On Friday the minister gave us some statistics. For the $15 million the federal government is intending to spend, he said there had already been submitted accepted projects totalling $57 million, of which he claimed that 38 per cent would be in labour expenditure. The federal government's share of that amount, he said, would come to $7,751,000. Even accepting the minister's estimates, this federal government is offering to pay some $7 million out of an expenditure of $57 million. Mr. Chairman, this does not look to me as though this government is accepting much responsibility, when the offer is made to our hard-pressed municipalities that this government will spend $7 million if the municipalities will agree to spend $50 million out of their own resources.
Again accepting the minister's figures, we find that he says this will give employment of 1,226,358 man days. Dividing this figure by five, then dividing it by four and dividing it again by five months, according to the minister's own estimate we find it producing aid to 12,264 men for five months. I hope the minister will explain how at the beginning of his talk he predicted employment for over 20,000 men if half this money was going to be spent, indicating indirectly employment for 40,000 men. Taking the number of man days he mentioned, dividing by five because there are five work days in the week, and dividing by four because there are four weeks in the month, and then dividing by five again because five months is the average period this project is intended to serve, you come to only 12,264 men for a five-month period. That is taking the minister's own estimate and the number of man days of employment that are going to be given.
Supply-Labour
Even taking the minister's own estimate we must come to the conclusion that only 5 per cent, and not more than 5 per cent at most, of the unemployed in Canada are going to receive assistance from this measure. It is hardly sufficient in this day and age for a federal government of Canada to say to 100 unemployed men, "Look, we cannot help you all; we will help five out of the one hundred." That is hardly in keeping with concepts and expectations that have been built up in Canada over many long years now, beginning with the green book offer of 1945 that the federal government should assume all responsibility for all employable unemployed in Canada. It is certainly not in line with the expectations that were raised among the Canadian electorate before the election of either 1957 or 1958.
We now get the advice, "Yes, you will get a little bit of help from Ottawa, provided you are prepared to load a fantastic tax burden on the homes of Canadians living within your municipality". That is in effect what this offer amounts to. The minister is offering $7 million if municipal councils are willing to saddle the home owners with a debt burden of $50 million. That is what this offer amounts to, based on the minister's own estimate. Even if his estimate is right, I maintain that this is expecting far too much of our municipal officials, who have reached about the limit of the taxes they can impose back home where the debt burden of the municipalities is coming close to the maximum.
I should like to refer to one statement made by the minister as reported at page 1018 of Hansard. He stated in effect that this plan was evolved out of a meeting on unemployment called last summer, and a later meeting with the mayors and reeves of our municipalities. Referring to the municipal officials who were in Ottawa he had this to say, as reported at page 1018 of Hansard:
In other words, they felt they could proceed with some of their municipal projects in the winter time provided the additional cost was offset by a contribution from the federal government.
It may well have been that when the minister urged the municipalities to undertake public works in the winter months, they put before him the argument that winter construction costs are higher, and the idea may have been expressed that some compensation ought to be paid. However, I am sure the mayors and reeves never meant to convey the idea that, as municipalities, they were willing to assume the burden of unemployment relief works and that all they were asking was that the extra costs caused by winter weather should be borne by the federal government. These figures I have spoken

Supply-Labour
of indicate that all Ottawa seems prepared to do is to carry the extra burden caused by our inclement winter weather. Mr. Chairman, this whole program is too small a share of too limited a program, arriving much too late in the season to be of any major assistance in the matter of unemployment.

May I ask a question of the
hon. member who has just sat down. When the hon. member mentioned that only 10,000 men were going to be employed with the money voted by the federal government, did he take into account the number of persons who would be employed in the industries supplying the materials and machinery to do this work in the cities of Canada?

Yes, I did. I indicated why,
and I also had a full appreciation-and I said so in my remarks had the hon. member been listening-of the claim of the minister that for every one directly employed there would be three employed in off-site jobs, and I am not arguing with that at all.

Mr. Chairman, I wish only to take a moment, because this legislation under discussion will most certainly pass. I would like to suggest to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat that it should not to be construed to this house or to the people of Canada that there is any general dissatisfaction with this item. I have here one example, and there are many others. This is a letter from the Calgary labour council; a member of a body which I believe my hon. friends are intending to court, with apparently no success as yet, in the labour movement of Canada. In the opening paragraph this letter states very clearly that they commend the government for taking this action, and in a subsequent paragraph they say that they feel the result of this policy is good. In the Calgary area approximately $2J million will be approved, which will of course materially help to reduce unemployment. That is but one example.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

Yes, when I
am through.
I only wanted to ask, would he table the letter?

Yes, I will be very happy to do so. As I was saying, this is but one example of the attitude of a great number of organizations in connection with the success of this program. I think the house must keep in mind that this is but one of the moves which are being made to answer,

at least in part, the problem of unemployment as it faces Canada today. It is not a whole program in itself but only a contribution to it.
I think, too, Mr. Chairman, while I am on my feet I would like to make a suggestion in recognition of the problem as it affects certain areas, based on their climatic conditions or geographical position in our country. I think any future consideration of a program of this type should keep in mind that it is difficult, with sub-zero temperatures, to take full advantage of the offer which in effect is going to require the extensive supplying of concrete for sidewalks and other works which can be included in this entire program.
I also have a letter from the association of professional engineers. They make a suggestion which I think is worth while to consider, that the construction of roads and streets being to some extent impracticable because of climatic conditions in certain areas, such construction work as building homes for the aged and hospitals should be considered. In other words, Mr. Chairman, what I am suggesting is that some flexibility in a future program of this type should recognize the difficulty which exists in sub-zero areas of Canada taking complete and full advantage of the suggestions which were offered, I believe very generously, by the government.
I also think, in the same sphere, that consideration should be given to providing assistance in the development of plans and engineering designs, because many municipalities will not have undertaken at an early stage some of the major projects upon which they would like to commence work. These two suggestions I offer in the hope that if a future offer is made in any other year, considerations can be given to them.

Mr. Chairman, I know all the members of the house will agree with me when I say that I think one of the greatest catastrophes which could befall any person is the loss of employment whereby he or she provides the means of subsistence for his or her family. It is for that reason, Mr. Chairman, that I want to say a few words in regard to this item.
I think I can speak with some feeling, without boasting whatsoever, because I have had some experience as mayor of Niagara Falls. I think the Minister of Labour will agree with me when I say that one of the drawbacks and one of the reasons we have to prepare some sort of plan for winter unemployment is the fact that automation has stepped in. The advanced machinery age has stepped in, which deprives a lot of men of work throughout the winter. It was not too many years ago when in

Niagara Falls, when we had a snowstorm, we would hire about 200 to 250 men and take quite a few days clearing the snow away. Now with three snow loaders and a number of trucks we can do the same job with 10 or 12 men, and they certainly take the place of manpower.
I think one of the things we must impress upon ourselves is that too many people are looking to the higher levels of government, rightly so or not, for work to be provided. I believe this is a co-operative affair. I feel that the municipalities, the provincial governments and the federal government must cooperate; and not only that but industry, whether large or small, and municipalities must also co-operate in this matter.
There are certainly a lot of jobs that can be done, as the previous speaker said, in the winter but which are done either in the spring, summer or fall. I have a friend who is a large contractor. He always said to me, and I will never forget it, "I try to do the jobs in the summer which I can do. There are only two jobs I can't do in the winter, and they are anything in regard to soil and outside painting. I do the construction, the basic work, in the summer and fall and leave the inside work for the winter so I can provide employment for my men". I was also talking to another contractor, who said, "I try to hire men who have a dual capacity as mason and plasterer. I do the work outside in the summer and fall, the masonry, the soil and painting work, and then I put these masons plastering and painting inside during the winter."
I think this is all bogey talk. We hear so many people say you cannot do a certain job in the winter, that it must be done in the summer. Manufacturers as well as governments have to learn that almost 90 per cent of the jobs can be done in the winter as well as summer.
What does the Department of Labour say about seasonal unemployment? The Department of Labour refers to seasonal unemployment regarding economic and social waste in these terms:
Seasonal unemployment in real terms means Inability to utilize available manpower and productive capacity and maladjustments in the allocation of resources, all of which impose additional cost on the economy.
Seasonal unemployment, like most any other type, creates a feeling of insecurity and dissatisfaction on the part of those who bear it most directly.
Mr. Chairman, it has been said by the hon. member for the C.C.F. party that there are some objections to this plan. In the first place, it is too little and it is too late. In the second 66968-8-69
Supply-Labour
place, a lot of the municipalities cannot afford it. In the third place, many municipalities are not taking proper advantage of it even if they can afford it. But I think a point which is of paramount importance is the fact that municipalities cannot afford the supplies. If the government had included supplies I am sure many, many more municipalities would have taken advantage of this program.
Now, I want to say to the Minister of Labour that I think he did a very fine thing when he called that conference last July. I congratulated him at that time, because I thought it was a proper thing to do with unemployment coming, as it was sure to, this winter. But people who attend conventions, and I have been to plenty of them, go to them full of pep and enthusiasm and say, "Oh, yes, we will do this and we will do that". They pass all kinds of resolutions about what they intend to do, but the moment the door of the conference hall is closed behind them they lose their enthusiasm and lose the vigour with which they were holding forth about the ideas promoted at the convention.
If there is one criticism which can be made of the minister it is this. It can certainly be said of him that he was too late in getting the instructions out to the municipalities. My colleague the hon. member for Essex East asked on a number of occasions in August if a report had been received by the cabinet in connection with this convention, and the minister replied that it had not. The municipalities received a telegram from the Prime Minister in the last week of October. We on this side certainly thought the conference should have been held in time to enable plans to be formed. Plans should have been in the hands of the various municipalities by the end of September at the latest, because the municipal governments must know on what basis they are to plan, they must study their budgets and be given information as to what lies ahead. In this respect the Minister of Labour has a most important task on his hands.
May I offer this suggestion to the minister, and I do so with all possible friendliness; in fact, I should like to offer him two or three suggestions. First of all, he should call together the ministers of labour of the various provincial governments and have them meet here in Ottawa as soon as possible to talk over not only the question of winter unemployment but the subject of unemployment in general. The ministers of labour should then return to their provincial governments, call in the reeves and mayors of the various municipalities and discuss at once

Supply-Labour
with them the answer to the problem which is bound to be presented by unemployment next winter.
There is a further suggestion I should like to make to the minister, and I think it is a feasible one. The hon. member for Calgary South has referred here to work being carried on in April and May. We have this problem arising in Niagara Falls, namely that it is almost impracticable to undertake work on sidewalks and similar projects in the month of April. The same is true, I know, in other municipalities, and I hope the minister will endeavour to persuade the government to agree that this work can be carried on until at least June 1, in order that more municipalities may be able to take advantage of this provision and go ahead with their schemes.
I often wonder about this situation, and sometimes I shudder to think of it. Suppose the Liberal party were responsible for the government at the present time, and suppose unemployment were as high as it is today-* of course it would not be as high if the Liberals were in power. I shut my eyes and imagine how the Minister of Labour, in his genial way, would criticize us. Certainly the hon. lady who is now Minister of Citizenship and Immigration would be at our heels almost every day complaining about the situation as, I have no doubt, would the Minister of Finance. He would be doing his homework every night in an effort to find arguments to direct against us, using the same arguments that we are using now.
Hon. members opposite may ask us, what are you offering as a solution? Well, there are two or three suggestions which I am offering toward a solution, and with regard to the first of these I believe the Minister of Finance will be in agreement with me. This is an old chestnut. I have heard many fine speeches in this house and many fine arguments advanced in favour of the elimination of the automobile tax. The Minister of Finance certainly made some when he was in opposition, and I am sure if the government could see fit to remove this tax it would have splendid results in keeping men at work. Cars would at once become cheaper, and many more people would be buying them.
I should like to point out to the committee that there are almost half a million people connected with the automotive industry, which provides about one in ten of all the jobs available in the country. When one considers that we have in Canada over 5,000 automobile dealers, well over 15,000 independent garages and over 18,000 service stations, the importance of this industry to employment becomes apparent.

There is another thought which occurs to me, and perhaps in speaking about this I am being somewhat selfish because the problem arises in the Niagara district more acutely than anywhere else. We could put a lot of men at work in the Niagara district if it were not for the 25 per cent duty imposed by the United States government on crushed stone. If this duty could be removed at least half a million tons of crushed stone per year, and perhaps twice this amount, could be sold to a value of almost $1,500,000. This naturally would mean more winter work, more work for truck operators, loaders and others.
There is a large potential market for crushed stone in the United States, particularly in the Niagara Falls, Buffalo and Cleveland areas, but unfortunately with this 25 per cent duty we cannot compete. If the minister would get together with his counterpart in Washington with a view to eliminating this duty the result would go a long way toward eliminating unemployment in the Niagara district. The latest figures which are available to me show that in 1956 Canada imported from the United States crushed stone to the value of $1,162,900, while Canadian exports to the United States amounted to a little over $49,000. There is obviously room for Canada to benefit in this direction.
There is a further matter, and I believe the Minister of Finance will agree with what I have to say on this subject also, because he is as familiar with the subject as I am. I spoke about it during the debate on the speech from the throne. I believe one of the ways by which the federal government could help relieve unemployment would be by restricting the dumping and unfair importation of cutlery and plastics from the United States and Japan. In the last two weeks the silverware companies of Niagara Falls have had to lay off another 150 men, because no silverware made in Canada can possibly compete successfully against products manufactured at very low cost due to the poor wages and inhuman conditions governing the employment of Japanese workers.
I might point out that the soap companies, which as hon. members may know include prizes and premiums with their products, have not put into their packages a single piece of silver made by companies in Niagara Falls for a very long time, whereas two years ago they were buying large quantities of this merchandise from Niagara Falls. If we could recover this trade it would mean employment for 400 or 500 men.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I am sorry to have to remind the hon. member for

Niagara Falls that we are discussing a contribution toward labour costs by the federal government, not generalities or importations which are subject to customs and tariff duties.

Well, I will try to get the engine back on the track if I can. I appreciate your correction, Mr. Chairman, but I was pointing out one way of increasing employment in Niagara Falls. If these men are to be put back at work we must certainly offset the consequences of importing this type of product from Japan.
Winter unemployment, as I need hardly point out, has a most unfortunate moral effect. A man walks the streets all day and when he comes home his wife asks him, have you got a job? The man says he has failed to find work, and this is the cause of many wrecked homes. Many of our younger generation, after walking the streets looking for jobs in vain, are tempted to turn to occupations which are less than honest. The prisons are filled with people who were trying to find some substitute for honesty. If we could make more winter employment available it would go a long way toward coping with this problem.
I want to pay my respects to the government, and through the government to the Minister of Public Works. When the estimates were tabled a week or so ago I learned that they included provision for a new post office and a new unemployment insurance building in Niagara Falls. May I urge the minister to get the projects under way as soon as possible so the outside work may be done this coming summer and thus provide plenty of employment for workers in this area. At the same time I would urge him to start construction of the new post office at Stevensville, which would provide that small community with work during the winter. I know that the construction of two large buildings of this nature in Niagara Falls will assist in alleviating the unemployment problem there.
The worst thing that can happen to an employed man or an unemployed man is to become a victim of fear with respect to whether or not he can adequately provide for his family. The workers of Canada are contributing to the development of our country. We want them to feel a sense of justifiable pride in the work they are doing so they can throw back their shoulders and stick out their chests content in the knowledge that they are making a valuable contribution to the nation. It is important that they do not become victims of discouragement or fear. Above all we must not permit them to lose faith in Canada.

I wish to refer again to winter unemployment in Niagara Falls. I have in my hand a statement made by the mayor of Niagara Falls in his inaugural address delivered during the first week of January, in which he said:
In the beginning of 1958 there were 1,937 males and 1,042 females or a total of 2,979 persons registered at the local employment office for the area. Of the persons registered 2,880 were drawing assistance.
I might explain that the area embraces Niagara Falls, Chippewa and Stamford. The mayor went on to explain that as of December 24, 1958 there were 2,175 males and 1,248 females or a total of 3,423 persons registered, and of this total 3,272 persons were drawing assistance. This certainly indicates a very serious unemployment problem. He then went on to discuss the plans of the city of Niagara Falls concerning the construction of sewers and water mains at an estimated cost of $109,000, of which the city's share is $86,300, with a view to relieving the situation.
I believe it would be interesting to the committee to present a comparison of the portion of direct relief paid by the city, which of course is 20 per cent, to the amount received from the federal government through this plan designed to alleviate unemployment. I have prepared a table showing a breakdown of the construction of a 6-inch water main and a 24-inch sewer, showing the number of man hours of unskilled labour represented in each project, the amount to be paid by the city and the amount of direct relief paid by the city. There are countless opportunities for employment in Canada through the inauguration of various projects. Some 30 years ago Canada was just a child or a young boy. In the last 30 years our nation has grown to manhood, and is the envy and admiration of all countries of the world. Certainly the

Supply-Labour
payment of $15 million to provide employment represents just a peanut policy on the part of the government, if I may use that vernacular expression. I presume that with the share contributed by the provinces the payment will be in the neighbourhood of $30 million, which is still just a drop in the bucket.
We have heard much talk about vision. I hope all hon. members in this chamber have vision and I know they have, but vision must lead to concentrated and vigorous action in order to be effective. I know the Minister of Labour will certainly give us some action if he is permitted to do so. May I say to that hon. gentleman in a friendly spirit that I appreciate that he recognizes the plight of the unemployed. He represents a riding that has serious unemployment problems, and he is as familiar as any hon. member in this committee with the problems besetting his constituents.
May I use the parlance of the automobile industry in directing my next remarks to him, and I do so because his riding is the centre of a large automobile industry. In all seriousness I suggest to him that he should change the type of gasoline used in the machine of his department and in the cabinet of his government as well. Let us get the machine out of neutral and put it into high. If I were in his place I would start feeding the members of the cabinet tranquilizing pills. I realize that all ministers are proud and jealous of their departments, but in my opinion the department of the Minister of Labour is one of the most important in the federal government. I believe he is doing an excellent job in his department, but he is running up against a bulwark of jealousy in the cabinet because some of the ministry are jealous of their departments and want more money for them.
The minister has shown a great deal of fighting spirit within this chamber in the last few weeks, and I urge him to take that kind of spirit into the cabinet and demonstrate to the other ministers that there is a need of more money for unemployment relief projects. If this were done I am sure the minister would win the gratitude of all Canadians.
In all seriousness I say that the workers who are contributing to the building of Canada today have the same spirit that animated their forefathers of old when they molded a great dominion out of a vast wilderness. However, the Canadian workman must have his fear of unemployment dispelled. He must

be offered the encouragement of increased employment opportunities in order to make Canada the great nation it potentially is.

I should like to make a couple of comments about this particular item from the point of view of the effect it has on the constituency I represent and its effect generally. The first indication that the country had that such a program was going to be entered into was a telegram from the Prime Minister to the various provinces. I think we should attempt to analyse what the basic design behind that telegram was in addition to letting the provinces know that the federal government was willing to enter into projects of this type on a cost-sharing basis. What it was designed to do-and it did this- was to leave the impression with the general public that the federal government was going to participate in 50 per cent of the costs with the municipalities on certain types of projects.
Labour costs.

My hon. friend can take his own time to make his own speech on his own feet without interrupting me and misinterpreting what I say. The impression that was left in the country was that the federal government was going to participate by paying 50 per cent of the cost of municipal projects.
Labour costs.

You can talk about labour costs all you want to, but that was the impression that was left with the general public, namely that the federal government was

going to bear 50 per cent of the costs. Then when the letter from the minister was sent, we found the gimmicks in this program and the loopholes and we found out that the federal government were not so generous as they originally let on they were. We found out what this so-called 50 per cent means in terms of the amount of money that will be contributed. That matter has been dealt with at some length by others in this debate. But from the minister's own figures we find that the federal government is going to contribute 13 per cent of the costs. I assume that the minister's figures are correct even though he may have misinterpreted the information which was given to him by the municipalities. As I say, we find that the federal government will pay 13 per cent of the cost of these projects and that the municipalities, already deep in debt, will be bearing 87 per cent of the cost.
There are three reasons why this is not a too sensible approach in so far as municipalities are concerned. Certainly it affords some employment to people presently unemployed. One reason is that it was too late in the year, too close to the winter season to make proper preparation for such type of work. The second was that many municipalities were completely involved because of their project arrangements. They had laid their plans out for the year sometime previously.
The third question is their debt position. We all know the position of the municipalities and we know that they vary from one to the other. But generally speaking, the fact is that they have been going deeper and deeper into debt as the years have gone by. This apparent benevolence on the part of the government in this respect was not what it was originally represented to be. It merely means that the municipalities carry the large burden of the costs, paying almost the complete amount toward projects of this type, and the federal government comes along and takes the credit. This is something which it has been quite willing to do in many other cases in the past, namely to take credit for something as long as somebody else pays for the program and does the work.
In the constituency of Skeena this program means relatively little. I am sure the minister has had communications from municipalities to the effect that, generally speaking, they are not able to participate in a program of this type for a variety of reasons.
I should like to make reference to a couple of communications I have from municipalities out there in order to show precisely how little this program means to the municipalities in that constituency. While my friend and

fellow westerner, the hon. member for Calgary South, made some reference to a letter he had received-I believe it was from the Calgary labour council-to the effect that this was a generous program, I submit that possibly the Calgary labour council is not as close to the situation as are the municipalities themselves to which I should like to make reference. I have here a letter from the corporation of the village of Burns Lake. It is dated January 21, 1959, and reads in part as follows:
It is felt that, as the federal government shares only in the direct payroll costs of any project, the benefits to the municipality are negligible.
Consequently they are not able to undertake any type of project. I also have a letter from the corporation of the district of Kitimat. It is dated January 19, 1959, and, with respect to the winter works program, it reads in part as follows:
The program was announced so late in the year that it was impossible for us to take advantage of it before the rigours of winter were upon us . . . It is a pity it could not have been announced two or three months earlier so that the procedural details would have been worked out in time to take advantage of some of the earlier winter months.
We have these two municipalities in my own constituency which express the point of view with respect to this program. They are far closer to the scene than were those to whom my hon. friend referred who wrote to him from Calgary.

65,000	to 70,000 people being employed in these winter works projects throughout Canada. That is based on the projects which have already been approved, as I understand it. If I am incorrect I am sure the minister will take advantage of the situation to correct the figures.
Twenty-two thousand.

No; I understood 22,000 were directly involved, and then he tripled that. His reference was to three times that figure; and at an earlier stage of the proceedings in the house he made reference to 60,000 people being employed either directly or indirectly. It was that 60,000 or 70,000 figure to which I am making reference. Hearing no objection from the minister, I assume I am fairly close to what his figures were in that regard.

effect that the housing program of the government last year resulted in some 200,000 man-years of employment, which he interpreted to mean 400,000 jobs provided. If this is so, I am not complaining about that part of it one bit; it is quite laudable. But I suggest that the government, out of its own mouth, condemns itself for its shortsighted policy when it comes to dealing with unemployed people of this nation. It has not the foggiest idea where it is going so far as economic problems are concerned, and is only able to make small, faltering steps to correct it by instituting something like the winter works program, or something similar to the housing program which comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works.
The other day we had an announcement from the dominion bureau of statistics to the effect that 538,000 people were out of work seeking employment. They are the figures which the minister attaches himself to as being the lowest of the group of figures compiled by that department. If we add to this the estimated number of people who are being employed as a result of the winter works project, and the estimated number that the Minister of Public Works suggested would be employed as a result of the housing program, we find ourselves with the D.B.S. figure of somewhere in the neighbourhood of
800,000	or 900,000 people out of work. I am not saying what the unemployment insurance figures would be, but they would be much higher than that.
This arises for one reason, because the government fails to see precisely what the problem is, just as our friends failed to recognize what the problem was when they were in office. This arises because continually over the years Canadian parliaments-perhaps not in toto but certainly recent parliaments- gave away in many cases control of sections of our economy to private individuals and private groups, and let them go their own merry way without too much thought or concern about the effect it would have on society or the economy generally. When we get into economic difficulties because we have given away the operation and control of our society and economy to outside sources, everyone comes running to the government to bail them out, and the Canadian taxpayer bears the brunt by paying for the mistakes and errors of the private individuals who control the country. We end up increasing the debt, borrowing more money and selling more bonds in order to promote a winter works program and housing development, only because governments in the past, and this government at present, failed to realize that someone else is controlling and directing the

Supply-Labour
economy. It should be their responsibility when they are in office, representing the taxpayers of the nation.
The minister also made reference to the planning which is necessary in order to cope with these things. I suggest to the minister that he should not be afraid of words like planning or co-ordination, but should realize, as I am sure he does, that it is necessary; and unless we have some sort of plan or coordination of our economic system we are going to continue to have economic difficulties from time to time. I know that the minister basically, deep down inside himself, is a sort of socialist, if I may put it that way. He is a socialist-minded person, but there are too many arch Tories in the cabinet and he cannot get his point of view across. That is the whole difficulty. I know that if the minister had his way and was able to institute the type of economic system necessary to deal with these things, and was able to have the influence which he would like to have in getting his points of view across- perhaps even if he were the minister of finance-we would be in a much better position than we are at the moment, because then the minister could deal with the question of employment as it should be dealt with. It would not be done in this haphazard, halfway measure by sending telegrams, and things like that. The minister could exert a little more pressure and could even threaten to resign a couple more times, perhaps, than he has already. Then perhaps he would be able to move the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance a little more in the direction of dealing in a sensible fashion with this problem, and institute some sort of planning in order to ensure that our taxpayers and the working-class people of this country do not recurrently find themselves on the unemployment rolls, and the federal government does not have to come to the assistance, not only of the people unemployed but of private industry and bail them out, plunging the Canadian taxpayer further into debt by so doing.

May I ask
the hon. member a question, who was talking of private enterprise. Is it the policy of his party that they would take over the industries in Canada which he was referring to?

If you continue to interject and not give me an opportunity to answer the question I shall resume my seat. If my hon. friend had been paying attention to political affairs and studying the different

political philosophies over the years, he would not have to ask such an asinine question.

GORE DISTRICT MUTUAL FIRE INSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-7, respecting Gore District Mutual Fire Insurance Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to change the name of the Gore District Mutual Fire Insurance Company to the Gore Mutual Insurance Company. The company's present name is not sufficiently descriptive of the types of insurance business it now carries on. You will notice that the words "district" and "fire" are dropped. This company was formed and originally established in 1839 by an act of the crown which permitted the creation of a fire insurance company in the various districts into which the province of Ontario was then divided. Those districts included London district, Wellington district including Guelph and the Gore district which embraced an area taking in Hamilton, Dundas, Galt and Brantford.
The Gore District Mutual Fire Insurance Company began business in the area from which it derived its name 120 years ago and after these many years the company does business throughout the province of Ontario and in addition has for a considerable number of years conducted substantial business

in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. The company also maintains branch offices in each of these provinces.
The word "district", which has a historical significance, is now no longer applicable to this company and is detrimental in that it frequently gives the impression that the company is something other than a national institution. The directors believe that the company would be more adequately named if the word "district" were dropped.
The same story applies to the word "fire". Originally in 1839 the company was established as a purely fire insurance company. Since that time, however, the federal government has authorized the company to write all types of insurance except life. In fact, over 60 per cent of the business of the company is now derived from other than fire insurance. The dropping of the word "fire" is in line with the practice of other companies which have experienced the same sort of growth and expansion.
I might mention that the federal superintendent of insurance, Mr. MacGregor, has been kept informed of the proposed change and believes it to be appropriate. The company has had a wonderful record of service over the past century and has contributed many thousands of dollars to charitable causes. I might mention here that during world war I the Gore District Mutual Fire Insurance Company made an outright grant of $100,000 to the federal government to aid in the war effort.
This bill is a very simple request on the part of a progressive company with a very fine and patriotic background, and in my humble opinion it should be passed with the minimum of delay so that the company may carry on its fast growing business under the name of the Gore Mutual Insurance Company, the proper name for the type of business being carried on at the present time by this long established institution.

In this morning's Globe and Mail Robert Duffy makes the statement that "parliament has the authority to pass bills of divorce on any grounds it chooses." In my opinion that is a rather general statement and I do not believe that could be done without further action by the house. For the time being we have to deal with a certain type of evidence and certain essentials required to establish grounds for a divorce. I suggest to hon. members that the manner of handling divorce cases should not differ from the way in which they are handled in the appropriate courts in the various jurisdictions throughout the country. I believe that there should be some uniformity of practice and requirements.
I think that the essentials of a divorce may be summarized briefly as follows: First of all, there is the question of jurisdiction; second, proof of misconduct; third, the questions of connivance, condonation and collusion; and, fourth, proof of marriage, etc. In his earlier reference to this question the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Mc-Cleave) spoke about the question of jurisdiction and the danger of possible abuses of the process of law through parliament in the presenting of petitions to this house which more properly should have been presented in courts of provincial jurisdiction. In the past cases have been presented before the house and the committee where marriages had not been proved and previous divorces had not been proved, and as far as practice was concerned they left much to be desired.
The hon. member spoke about proof of adultery and the weight of evidence required. I do not think I should have to go over that ground but I should like to deal now with the questions of connivance, condonation and collusion. In this connection I should like to refer to a very valuable authority, "The Law of Divorce in Canada", by W. Kent Power, published in 1948. The author of that learned text speaks about connivance at pages 41 and 42, and for the guidance of members of the house I should like to put on the record the principles by which we should be

guided in considering these cases. In dealing with connivance, the book says this:
Connivance means that the adultery of one spouse has been caused by or has been knowingly, wilfully or recklessly permitted by the other as an accessory. It must precede the offence, and is clearly distinguishable from condonation which follows it.
I quote further:
Connivance implies that the plaintiff has been accessory to the very offence on which the action is based, or at least has corruptly acquiesced in its commission.
In the event that there should be connivance, that is a fatal flaw to the petition in my humble submission. Members of this house should scrutinize the evidence presented for any suggestion of connivance just as carefully as they would for any other point.

But all the elements of connivance are here, and none of the elements which would disprove connivance are present. I think this woman knew that this was going on, and I do not think she did anything about it until it was suitable for her to petition for a divorce.
Another question I should liked to have asked her concerns her present financial position. It came out in the evidence that from the time these two people were married the wife earned more money than her husband. As far as I can see she is still earning more money than her husband. The petition for this divorce would, therefore, certainly not be on support grounds, because this woman is quite capable of supporting herself. It is obvious that up till now the woman has not felt herself to be morally wrong. Apparently she had no pangs of jealousy until six years after the marriage, and I cannot help but feel that behind her petition for divorce is a desire to enter into another alliance. This woman could not be asked this question but it is certainly fair for anyone sitting on the committee and reading the evidence to ask himself: is this a bona fide case where a woman wronged by adultery has come before this committee for a hearing, expecting us to give her the benefit of our doubts.
There can be no question that there is doubt in this case. The woman is asking for the benefit of this doubt. In order to get this benefit I suggest she has to come to us with clean hands. It is obvious that if she is guilty of connivance or condonation we would refuse the petition. If she were asking us to grant the petition on humanitarian grounds because she is distressed, that might cause us to bend in her direction and give her the benefit of any doubt, but I claim that in this case all the evidence is negative.
She has not satisfied me. She may have satisfied the committee. Of course, it is up to everyone to decide according to his own conscience whether or not he believes there has in fact been condonation or collusion. However, from my point of view, speaking for myself and apparently for the other members of this committee-the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in particular-we should be very careful to make sure that everything has been done before we grant this petition. I see no reason why we should not send the bill back, because it is a very serious matter to dissolve this marriage, and we should not be doing our duty to the two people concerned, or perhaps to the three people concerned, if we did not see everything was done to preserve this marriage and give it every chance.

I cannot believe that two days is long enough for any woman to consider the question of adultery even if it had been committed. I am quite sure that many marriages would be broken up if such haste was the order of the day. Many marriages have been saved after one of the parties has fallen from grace. It would not be hard to go through cases in civil law and find instances where marriages have been saved by time. I do not know whether any attempt was made by either party to effect a reconciliation. The husband did not appear before us and the question was never put to the wife. Certainly, two days is not long enough, and it was this two-day limit which began my suspicion concerning this whole case. Knowing the difficulty of getting attention through legal channels, I found it astounding that a woman should, after suddenly being confronted with the adultery of her husband have a petition before the Senate within two days of the alleged offence.
I notice there are no children involved in this case and that is a blessing in a marriage apparently as unhappy as this one. Since no children are involved, this would simplify a settlement of any property after the marriage is finally dissolved, if and when it is dissolved. But let us suppose there had been children. This would have complicated matters very greatly. This has put the red light on again in our deliberations.

Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned at five o'clock, I was talking about the unemployment situation in our municipalities and saying how little the government has done to improve the situation. In reply to some questions asked by some 
hon. members, I shall refer to what certain ministers had to say, when they were in the opposition, about employment in Canada. When the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) had the floor, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) seemed to consider the whole thing as rather funny. However, I remember that during the 1955 session, as recorded on page 3396 of Hansard, he said:
(Text):
The second problem which has been ignored by the government is the problem of unemployment. This problem has been discussed at length in this session, or I would seek to go into it at greater length today. But let me content myself, in this limited time, with making this limited observation on the subject, that the government throughout this session has observed a conspiracy of silence in regard to unemployment.

When we were saying that the situation was serious, that it was getting worse from day to day and that the winter would be tough, we were accused of being crepe hangers, of exaggerating the situation; and yet, if we look at the latest statistics, we note that in January, the number of unemployed had risen by 11,000 across the country. This means an increase of 11,000 unemployed over last year's figure and a further increase compared to the figure for the previous year. In other words, if the government keeps on behaving as it now does, the situation will become absolutely unmanageable.

I hope the government will eventually wake up, as the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) said; in fact, he claimed that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) was well disposed, but that he had no co-operation from his cabinet colleagues. About the payment of half the cost of winter works, when I said that the cost of

those works undertaken during winter could exceed by 12 per cent that of works done diming the summer, a certain member rose to say that engineers had given him figures showing that the difference could not be more than one per cent. Well, that is possible if the hon. member has those works done on stone. It is cheaper during winter to quarry the stone because there is no water; hence, there is no need for pumping machines; stone is a good conductor of heat and cold and blasting is easier; I also understand that a mechanical shovel can pick it up without the necessity of repeated blasting. But when works are done in the ground, during winter, it is much more expensive. At the time I was mayor of Hull, I found that jobs carried out late in the fall or in winter time are much more expensive.
Mr. Chairman, if municipalities have to pay 10 to 12 per cent more, it means that they stand to gain absolutely nothing, because the cost of the labour required to carry out these jobs represents at most about 25 per cent of total costs at the present time. Anyway, the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) proved it this afternoon when referring to works undertaken in Quebec city.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the government should wake up and do something.
The other day I heard the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) state that out of 3,000 unemployed in that city, 48 only were helped through the winter works program in that locality. And it is the same almost everywhere. That is why the winter works program organized by the minister has been quite ineffective in Canada.
I hope that the minister will change his mind and that he will be able to convince the Minister of Finance and especially the Prime Minister, that superman who, before the election, promised to solve every problem. Mr. Chairman, it is with some regret that I break into this amusing little game of the pot calling the kettle black. However, I should like to confine my remarks today to the matter before the house at this moment. I think possibly a good place to start would be with the statement of the minister as found at page 1018 of Hansard of Friday, February 13, starting at the bottom of the page:
I do not know whether there is anything else I can add at the moment except to say that this

is a field in which the federal government has never before participated.
I have not taken the opportunity of searching back through Hansard in order to verify that statement. I can only presume that it is true because, while I followed all of the speeches made by members of the official opposition, to date I found nobody who has denied that statement by the minister. On this fact I should like to compliment the minister. It shows that he has realized that there is a situation that needs attention; his position is in contrast with that of many of his colleagues. It also shows that he is willing to go ahead and try something that has never before been tried by the government of this country.
I believe that what we should do now is to pay particular attention to this program he has started and see just how good it is, how well it meets the situation, whether it should be improved or enlarged or whether in fact it might not be better, in the interests of all concerned, if something else were substituted for it.
Mr. Chairman, there appears to be a certain amount of confusion among the various municipalities across the country with regard to this program. I think it is quite easy to realize why this is so. Contained in the original letter that went out from the minister to the various provincial premiers, on page 2 under the item "Terms of the Offer" we find the following:
The Canadian government, subject to the approval of the plan by the provincial government, will reimburse each municipality one-half of the direct payroll costs of the municipality or its contractors or subcontractors during the period from December 1, 1958, to April 30, 1959-
Yet on page 3, under the item marked No. 7, we find the following:
Payments to year-round employees of the municipalities will not be included as part of the direct payroll costs-
I think that is rather an important item and I think that is possibly one of the major reasons why confusion has been caused among the various municipal officials with regard to this plan.
I recall very well, Mr. Chairman, that when this plan was first announced with due fanfare and publicity the impression very definitely was created, first of all that the federal government was assuming 50 per cent of the costs of these projects. I grant that the government never said that, but the fact still remains that that impression was created. Certainly the municipalities welcomed this announcement with great good cheer. However, when they started going into the actual terms of this proposal they found that definitely was not the picture at all. Instead of finding the situation to be

in accord with the first impression they received, namely that the federal government was to undertake 50 per cent of the costs, they found that the 50 per cent which the federal government was going to share in was confined to the payroll costs. They found further that it was confined to the payroll of people who were not in the steady employment of the municipalities.
Again, in the minister's statement of the other day, as reported at page 1018 of Hansard, we find the same thing:
This program involved participation by the federal government to the extent of 50 per cent of the total payroll costs in such projects as would not ordinarily be undertaken during the winter.
In the same letter which the minister sent to the provincial premiers, in item No. 4 on page 3, it is stated:
The bulk of those employed under this plan must be unemployed at the time they are hired.
I presume it is intended to grant employment and the resulting wages to those most in need. But when I inquired among various municipal officials in the Timmins area they informed me-and apparently they must have been mistaken because certainly this is contained in this letter or directive-that they had the impression that the only people who could qualify on these jobs were unemployed whose unemployment benefits had completely run out. As I say, they may have been mistaken. Apparently either my informants were in error or else the people who supplied the minister with his information were in error, one of the two.
I certainly do not question for a moment the words of the minister. I am sure he based them on the information supplied him by his officials. I see again on the same page of Hansard, page 1018, where the minister says that, to their pleasant surprise, the labour content amounted to some 38 per cent of the cost of the projects. There again that information is very much at variance with the information supplied by some of the various municipal officials and contractors in my area.
Let me refer to the three main projects, or I should say categories, listed under here as follows. The categories of work projects to be covered, subject to the acceptance of each winter works project, are:
<a) The construction and major reconstruction of streets, sidewalks or roads, other than arterial roads;
(b)	The construction and major reconstruction of water, sewage and storm sewage facilities not including buildings;
(c)	The construction and development of municipal parks.
I have talked with various contractors and asked them what proportion of jobs particularly falling under the first two categories
