here would be involved in materials, and they informed me that on projects of this kind as high as 70 and 75 per cent of the cost of these projects would be for materials alone. They told me, of course, that under the terms of this agreement none of that cost would be shared by the federal government. They told me further that up to another 20 or more per cent would go for the cost of machinery-bulldozers, trucks, shovels, and that sort of thing. Again the federal government does not share these costs. Their share is confined to the cost of labour other than the regular municipal employees who may have to be placed on these projects to supervise them. In fact, they went so far as to say, particularly under these first two categories, that the actual labour cost that the federal government might share in would amount to not much more than 3 per cent of the cost of the whole project. As I say, possibly the information given to me is wrong, but that is the information I have.
In regard to this 50 per cent cost of payroll on jobs of this nature, such as sewage lines, water lines, trunk sewers and so on, it is impossible for the municipality just to go down to the employment office and hire 50 or 100 men and turn them loose on these projects. They must place their own experienced personnnel in charge of these projects; otherwise the repairs to these projects could cost more than the actual projects themselves.
So you can see, Mr. Chairman, that a considerable amount of the actual labour cost in these projects would involve permanent employees of the municipalities. They would have to put their engineers to work and their foremen on the job, and put leaders in charge of whatever projects they were working on. In fact, one of the municipal officials told me-and incidentally this is not contained under these three categories, so I am pleased to see that the government is not holding them down strictly to the three projects mentioned here-about a job concerned completely with manual labour in connection with clearing brush on a site which was going to be used as a city dump. All that was needed was an axe and a saw to cut the brush, and a box of matches to burn it. Under this project, which involved only manual labour, no machinery or material of any kind, they told me that all the municipality would realize from the contribution of both the federal government and the provincial government would be in the neighbourhood of 35 per cent.
There appears to be a lot of confusion. Either these people have the wrong impression or have been given the wrong picture

Supply-Labour
of this project, or else the figures supplied by the Minister of Labour are not in keeping with what the municipalities say in this project.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me to give him this information, Mr. Chairman. The figures I have quoted regarding this plan have all been supplied by the municipalities themselves.
These figures come directly from the municipalities?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: That is right.

Then, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid the mystery deepens as we go along. The minister quoted some of the figures of the numbers of men who, it is hoped, will be placed in employment over the next two or three months; in fact, over the five month period of this project. I believe he mentioned the figure of 22,712 men totalling up to a grand total of 1,226,358 man-days. Again, Mr. Chairman, it is difficult to get any kind of clear picture to evaluate what this program actually does. The best we can do is take some kind of average, and on that basis I believe, according to my mathematics, it works out to an average of about $12.77 per day for a total of 54 days, which is in fact about two and one-half months of working days. That would be in keeping with the directive in this letter to the effect that people employed on these projects will be paid at the going rate. I think possibly the rate of $12.77 a day would be a pretty fair average across the country from coast to coast of the daily wage being paid.
But another thing which I hope the minister will be able to supply as soon as the information is available is some kind of pattern of the length of time these people will be employed. Will they be employed for two weeks, one month, two months, or will some of them be employed full time and others for a very limited period? Again using the law of averages, we find that if one-half of these people employed were employed for the full four months period, the other half would only average one month of employment.
Mr. Chairman, X think the big question is this: Just what kind of an answer is this? This, we find, is the first and only project that this government has put forth designed specifically for the relief of unemployment. They have done other things, such as housing, which has helped but was not designed basically to relieve unemployment.
Yes, they were.

They were never stated as such. If I may continue with my
[Mr. Martin (Timmins) .)
mathematical exercise and project this particular plan to its fullest extent, supposing we were to use this plan, or one very similar to it, for the full relief of unemployment today. We would find that over a period of five months we hope to have a total of 1,226,358 man-days. With the present unemployment, that means it is two days' work for the unemployed over a period of five months.
The minister quoted a figure in respect of the amount of money this is going to cost the municipalities, and he also gave an estimate of the amount that would be reimbursed to the municipalities by the federal government. These figures are, of course, estimated figures and probably no more exact than the ones I have given. The best we can do is to make certain assumptions, and we find that in order to put everybody who is now unemployed back to work on the lines of a plan similar to this, the municipalities would have to raise in five months time over and above their regular budgets a total sum of $2,330 million of which, on the basis which has been mentioned, they would receive reimbursement from the federal government amounting to $379 million. This applies to the same five-month period. If we extended the period to a full year we would find that the municipalities would have to raise $5,600 million over and above their regular budgets and that of this sum the federal government would reimburse them to the extent of a billion dollars, or an amount in that neighbourhood.
I do not think it is impossible for the federal government to raise this one billion dollars. After all, it is roughly 50 per cent of what we are now spending on obsolete weapons of defence. But I do say it is a physical impossibility for the municipalities to raise their share. It is a hopeless proposition. Not only would the municipalities have to raise their own share, but they would also have to raise, initially at least, the share of the federal government and the share of the provincial government where the province is taking part, because it is clearly stated that the municipalities must raise these funds and that they will be reimbursed eventually by the federal government and by the provincial government if the province is sharing in the program.
I do not know exactly what the situation is in all the various provinces across the country, but I have been given to understand that in Ontario unemployed persons whose eligibility for benefits has run out can turn to the municipalities and the municipalities have to raise only 20 per cent of their welfare payments, the other 80 per cent of the cost

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
being reimbursed in the ratio, I believe, of 40 per cent by the federal government and 40 per cent by the provincial government. As time goes on and as more and more unemployed persons become ineligible for benefit and are obliged to fall back on the municipalities, how can a municipality be expected to take part in such a plan as we have heard described, under which they have to raise the full amount required to put these people to work, when today they only have to pay 20 per cent of the cost of relief? It is very fine to get all these jobs done, and many municipalities have jobs waiting which they have been trying to get under way for years. Let us not forget, however, that municipalities have to strike their budgets at the beginning of the year, and where in the world can they raise this additional money to put such a plan into effect way back at the end of the year? I mention these things to show that it is an impossibility as far as the municipalities are concerned.
There is one other point which I should like to have explained and it arises in the very first paragraph of the terms of the offer contained in the letter sent to the premiers of each province dated October 29. The letter says: "The Canadian government, subject to the approval of the plan by provincial governments" will do various things. And we find, according to the Minister of Labour's own statement, that even to date only five out of the ten provinces are participating in this plan. I wonder if this is the best we can do for the municipalities? Even if they want to take advantage of this scheme they cannot do so apparently unless they first obtain the approval of the province, regardless of whether the province is sharing in the scheme or not. This is one more item in the proposal which tends to confuse the municipalities and which has probably prevented them from taking advantage of this plan, inadequate as it is.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to enter into this discussion but as mayor of a municipality I must say I was filled with alarm when I realized the growing number of the unemployed. When one considers it, $15 million is really only a drop of water in the bucket when it is remembered that 538,000 people are without employment at the present time and that over 800,000 are seeking work. If we relate this sum of $15 million to the total number of the unemployed-538,000-and if we take as a basis of our calculation the assumption that the average wage of a labouring person in Canada today is $12.50 a day, then we find that $15 million would supply work for 538,000 unemployed people for about two and a quarter
days. Hon. members will agree with me, I think, that this is not going to do very much to alleviate the suffering among the unemployed in Canada.
It is said that the government pays 50 per cent of the cost of labour. On a public utility project, labour cost averages about 20 per cent of the total cost. The proposal means, in effect, that the government would be contributing approximately 10 per cent of the total cost of the project. As a mayor I can tell the committee that the financial situation of the municipalities is such that very few of them can afford to undertake any project on the basis of a 10 per cent contribution. Many of the municipalities in Canada at the present time are on the verge of bankruptcy.
The high cost of financing and issuing debentures is preventing many of our municipalities from undertaking even the projects which carry the highest priority, whether they are given a 50 per cent grant or not. If the government would indicate that something might be done in conjunction with the provinces, and that the provinces would contribute the other half of the labour costs, it might be possible for the municipalities to undertake desirable projects and to pay for the necessary materials. It must be remembered that municipalities have only limited scope with regard to raising money through taxation. The amount of taxes raised by the municipalities approximates only 10 per cent of the total tax levied, with the result that it is very difficult for the municipalities to take advantage of this plan by undertaking the construction of any public utilities at the present time.
One should also take into consideration the demoralizing effect of the presence of a large amount of unemployment upon those who are still employed-the fear of losing a job, the fear of hunger, the despair and anxiety which the situation creates. Let everyone remember that the Prime Minister said in his election speeches that not one man would go hungry in this country if he was put into power. I think it is about time the government took some action so that these projects could be carried out, but not on a 10 per cent basis because there is scarcely a municipality in Canada which could undertake to carry out a project on such terms.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The indication my hon. friend has given of going back to an earlier period prompts me to rise on a point of order concerning the limits of debate on this item. May I point out that this item involves simply a further amount to be added to an appropriation which parliament made at the last session for the current fiscal year. The need for this additional amount of $630,000 arises from one cause and one cause only, namely that effective April 1 of last year, the first day of the new fiscal year, the amount of the subsidy paid on the movement of coal from the maritimes to markets in eastern Canada was raised by 50 cents a ton. That is the purport of this item in its entirety and therefore with great respect I submit that the kind of remarks upon which my hon. friend indicates he is embarking are not in order.
What we are dealing with here is an item on which parliament has already appropriated something over $8,500,000 for a purpose approved by parliament in principle. All we have involved in the item now under discussion is an addition to that same item of an amount sufficient to pay for the additional subsidy of 50 cents a ton on the coal moved from the maritimes to the markets of

central Canada. With respect, Mr. Chairman, I do not think an item so confined in its effect is any occasion for as extended a debate as that upon which my hon. friend appears to have embarked.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I anticipated that as usual the Minister of Finance would interfere and attempt to call the speaker to order. On the very point of order raised by the Minister of Finance, where we are voting an additional amount of $630,000, which means a payment of 50 cents a ton additional for the transportation of coal from the maritimes to central Canada, I want to state that the very purpose of my remarks is this. I will seek to prove to this committee that this amount is not sufficient. The payment of $630,000 will not take care of the situation. With all due respect to the remarks made by the minister I feel that my remarks are duly in order.
I was about to comment on a statement made in this house by the former prime minister the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent prior to the election of June 1957.

estimate. I will therefore request the hon. member for Gloucester to restrict his remarks to transportation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am prepared to abide by your ruling but it is exceedingly difficult for any speaker to limit his remarks to the transportation of coal alone. There is a reason for this item. This vote is to help subsidize the transportation of coal in order to take care of the surplus of coal that presently exists in the province of Nova Scotia. I shall limit my remarks to the question of coal only.
I was saying that the former prime minister stated in this house that he wanted these coal mines to be kept in operation because, as he said, we do not want coal mining towns of Nova Scotia to become ghost towns and that so far as he was concerned and to the extent his opinions may have carried weight in the decisions that were taken then we were not going to encourage substantial increases in the production of coal because we did not think it would be fair to future generations of Canada. Those were the words of a prime minister who, notwithstanding the critical significance and possible reaction of his remarks on the eve of a general election, would rather tell the truth than adopt the position of his opponents by making promises which he never could fulfil.
On February 28, 1958, when speaking at Coxheath, Nova Scotia, the present Prime Minister is reported to have appealed for a new mandate on the basis that his government had fulfilled every promise made to the electorate. The words of the Prime Minister on that occasion were these:
I now ask for a working majority so that together we can go forward into the future and build a great Canada.
Those were the words of the Prime Minister prior to the last election. I am sure that some hon. members, especially those from Cape Breton and elsewhere in Nova Scotia, recall this full page advertisement during the last campaign. In it I find the words, "Action today or regret tomorrow."

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief. I would not want to disappoint the hon. member for Gloucester by having no one from Nova Scotia on this side of the chamber speak on this item. I should like to congratulate the government and the appropriate minister on the subventions that have been paid and also on the provision of this additional amount which I understand has helped acquire markets in Belleville, Ontario, and has also landed coal as far east as Toronto. The landing of Nova Scotia coal in eastern markets is of great assistance.
I am sure the government is considering the problems confronting the coal industry which were so ably expressed by the hon. members for Villeneuve and Gloucester and that appropriate action will be taken in this regard.
May I conclude by saying that I am glad hon. members of the Liberal party from the maritime provinces and also from Quebec have seen fit to speak on this item.

1.	When the St. Lawrence seaway is opened to navigation what canals will be entrusted to the St. Lawrence seaway authority for operation?
2.	Has the St. Lawrence seaway authority been given title to and control of the Welland ship canal and lands adjacent thereto? If so, on what date?
3.	Has the St. Lawrence seaway authority been given title to and control of the Cornwall canal and lands adjacent thereto? If so, what area of the Cornwall canal is included in the transfer and on what date did it take place?
4.	What duties and responsibilities will hereafter be entrusted to the canals branch of the department of transport and will this branch remain where it is or be brought under the jurisdiction of the St. Lawrence seaway authority?
5.	To what division of the department of transport will the secondary canals of Canada be entrusted for operation?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister
of Transport):
1.	Pursuant to section 14 of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act it is proposed to seek authority of the governor in council to entrust to the authority the management and operation of the following canals: (a) that portion of the Ontario-St. Lawrence canals remaining in service after the flooding of the pool above the power dam at Cornwall; (b) Lachine canal; (c) Welland canal; (d) Sault Ste. Marie canal; (e) the Beauharnois canal.
2 and 3. Answered by 1.
4.	The canals division of the Department of Transport will continue to administer the St. Peters canal, Canso lock, Chambly canal and the St. Ours lock on the Richelieu river, St. Annes lock and Carillon-Grenville canals on the Ottawa river, the lands of the Old Beauharnois canal and Soulanges canal, the Rideau canal and Trent canal.
5.	Answered by 4.

4.	Did the government authorize the transfer of the flag of the Canadian National steamships vessels from Canadian to foreign registry? If so, for what purpose?
5.	Did the government authorize a retransfer of the flag to Canadian registry? If so, for what purpose?
6.	What did the transfer of the flag accomplish?
7.	Did the sale of the above vessels take place, and to whom?

10.	Where are each of the ships now?
11.	Since the date of the strike, for what length of time have these ships been immobilized?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister
of Transport):
1.	Prior to the date of sale the Canadian National Steamships owned eight vessels.
2.	July 4, 1957.
3.	The management of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited announced on May 21, 1958, its decision to abandon the service between Canada and the West Indies and to dispose of the ships by sale. The House of Commons was advised of this decision on the same date.
4.	A complete statement on the transfer by the company of the ships from Canadian registry was made in the House of Commons on November 11, 1957.
5 and 6. In announcing on May 21, 1958, the decision to abandon the Canada-West Indies service, the management stated that the registry of the eight vessels had been transferred from Trinidad to Canada for the purpose of the sale of the fleet.
7.	Yes. Banco Cubano del Comercio Exterior.
8.	Not to the knowledge of the management.
9.	In addition to the announcement on May 21a further statement was made in the house on August 12, 1958.
10.	At date of sale the eight vessels were anchored at Halifax. The last press reports to come to the attention of the management indicated that seven were in Halifax and one in Baltimore.
11.	So far as the management of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships is concerned-from the date of the strike, July 4, 1957, to the date of the sale, August 12, 1958, the ships were out of service.
